notes.title: Start here: one PATCH, traced through every layer
notes.body:
This course follows one request: a client updates a customer profile with a PATCH, and the guides trace it through each layer until it is saved and audited. Two ideas carry the whole course. First, **omitting a field is not the same as sending `false`**. Second, **who you are comes from the session, not from the JSON you send**.

Suggested reading order:

1. `astraupskill/README.md` for the glossary (canonical object, version adapter, rollout, audit row).
2. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`, which tells you which file to open first and in what order.
3. `02-CONCEPTS.md`, the short theory chapter. Read it twice; most quizzes come from it.
4. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`, the repair shown in code.
5. `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`, including the senior review table of extra findings.

Keep `src/lib/versioning/customer-profile-contracts.ts` open in a second window while you read. Almost every rule in the guides is a few lines in that file, and reading the real code is faster than memorising the prose.

excerpts.quote: API compatibility depends on preserving omission and false values, while authorization depends on trusted session context rather than caller supplied ownership.
Start from the route, then inspect the canonical adapter, service, repository, and response adapter in that order.

readMore.why: Which file does what, and the order to read them in.
The core theory: presence, compatibility and authority.

notes.title: Concept: the canonical model and why presence matters
notes.body:
The app supports two public API versions, v1 and v2. They name things differently: v1 has one `fullName` and an `active`/`inactive` status, v2 has a nested name and a richer lifecycle. Instead of teaching every layer about both, a **version adapter** turns each request into one internal shape, the **canonical** object. The service and repository only ever see that shape.

For updates, the adapter has one more job: keep track of what the caller actually sent. A PATCH means "change these fields and leave the rest alone". So a missing key and a key set to `false` mean different things, and the adapter must not blur them. That is why the update adapters start from an empty object and copy in only keys whose value is not `undefined`.

When you read `toCanonicalUpdateInput`, look for the pattern `if (x !== undefined) canonical.x = ...`. That one line, repeated per field, is the whole rule.

excerpts.quote: The canonical model is the stable seam: version-specific names and statuses should not leak into repository or service policy.
An omitted property means “leave the stored value alone.” It is different from an explicit false, empty string, or null.
if (modernPayload.email !== undefined) canonical.email = modernPayload.email;

notes.title: Concept: where authority comes from, and checking before writing
notes.body:
Two rules keep the data safe.

**Authority.** A request body is just data the caller typed. If it says `ownerId: "someone-else"`, that proves nothing. Identity comes from the session context, and the service decides whether that actor may touch the profile. The service repeats the checks itself so that code calling it directly (jobs, tests) gets the same protection as the HTTP route.

**Validate before each side effect.** A side effect is anything that changes the world: a repository write, an audit row, a metrics call. If a request is going to be rejected, it must be rejected before any of those happen, so a failed request leaves no trace.

The guides are also honest about limits: this demo builds its session from plain request headers and uses fake repositories, so it teaches the shape of the rules, not production security or database atomicity. The senior review in `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` lists where that matters.

excerpts.quote: The session identifies the actor, and the service checks whether that actor may create or mutate the owner’s profile. A caller supplied `ownerId` is data, not authority.
A rejected version must stop before service calls, and a rejected profile mutation must leave repository and audit records untouched.

readMore.why: The senior review table: findings beyond the PATCH path.

notes.title: Why a TRIAL profile comes back ACTIVE
notes.body:
v1 only knows two statuses, `active` and `inactive`. Reading a profile, `toLegacyStatus` squashes both ACTIVE and TRIAL into `active`. Writing it back, `fromLegacyStatus` turns `active` into ACTIVE, because v1 has no way to say "trial". So the round trip quietly ends the trial: the stored lifecycle becomes **ACTIVE**. The guide calls this intentionally lossy, and the senior review lists it as finding 5.

Why the others are wrong:
- **TRIAL, nothing written**: there is no "skip unchanged values" rule. The v1 update adapter assigns `lifecycleState` whenever `status` is present.
- **SUSPENDED**: only `inactive` maps to SUSPENDED. TRIAL is read as `active`, not `inactive`.
- **409 rejected**: nothing refuses this change. The mapping simply produces ACTIVE.

excerpts.quote: return state === "ACTIVE" || state === "TRIAL" ? "active" : "inactive";
return status === "active" ? "ACTIVE" : "SUSPENDED";
if (legacyPayload.status !== undefined) canonical.lifecycleState = fromLegacyStatus(legacyPayload.status);

notes.title: Why an email-only v1 PATCH carries only email
notes.body:
The v1 update adapter starts from an empty object. It only calls `splitFullName` when `fullName` is not `undefined`; otherwise `migrated` is `undefined` and the `if (migrated)` block that adds `givenName` and `familyName` never runs. Email is present, so it is copied. Status is absent, so no lifecycle key is added. The result is a patch with **only email**, which is exactly what "leave everything else alone" needs.

Why the others are wrong:
- **email and lifecycleState**: `lifecycleState` is only set when `status` is present. Nothing defaults it.
- **names copied from the stored profile**: the adapter never reads the stored profile at all. It only sees the payload.
- **familyName 'Unknown'**: the `Unknown` fallback lives inside `splitFullName`, which is not called when `fullName` is missing.

excerpts.quote: const migrated = legacyPayload.fullName !== undefined ? splitFullName(legacyPayload.fullName) : undefined;
if (migrated) { canonical.givenName = migrated.givenName; canonical.familyName = migrated.familyName; }

notes.title: Why an unknown version becomes a 500, not a 400
notes.body:
`buildApiContext` runs inside the `try` and throws a proper 400 `badRequest` for `v9`. Control jumps to `catch`. Because `apiContext` was never assigned, the fallback expression calls `getRequestedVersion(request)` again, and it throws the same error again. This time the throw happens inside the `catch` block, where there is no `try` around it, so it escapes the handler and Next.js answers with its own 500. The lesson: an error handler that repeats the failing step turns a clean error into a crash.

Why the others are wrong:
- **TypeError before the try**: the context is built inside the `try`; the problem is the second call in `catch`.
- **deliberate 500 for alerting**: the senior review calls this a bug (finding 2), not a design choice.
- **Zod and ZodError**: the version header is not parsed by Zod here, and the review traces the 500 to the repeated call.

excerpts.quote: } catch (error) { const fallbackVersion = apiContext?.version ?? getRequestedVersion(request);
The `catch` block then calls `getRequestedVersion(request)` again, which throws outside the `try`, so the caller sees a framework 500 instead of 400.

notes.title: Why the profile owner comes from the session
notes.body:
In the POST route, the third argument to `toCanonicalCreateInput` is `apiContext.session.userId`, and the adapter writes it into `ownerUserId`. The body is never asked who the owner is. The concepts chapter states the rule: a caller-supplied `ownerId` is data, not authority, and a CLIENT may only create a profile owned by its own session. The service must enforce this too, so direct callers cannot slip in a foreign owner.

Why the others are wrong:
- **the body's ownerId once Zod validates it**: Zod checks that a value is well-formed, not that the caller is allowed to claim it. Validation is not authorization.
- **body first, session as fallback**: that still lets any caller pick someone else as owner whenever they include the field.
- **the x-api-version header**: that header selects the contract version. It says nothing about identity.

excerpts.quote: const canonicalInput = toCanonicalCreateInput( apiContext.version.id, body, apiContext.session.userId );
Ownership is also authoritative: a CLIENT session may create only a profile owned by that session, regardless of what a direct caller supplies.

notes.title: Why a metrics failure after a save hurts the client
notes.body:
In POST, the profile is created first, then the route builds the 201 response, then it **awaits** `recordVersionUsage` before returning. If that call throws, execution jumps to `catch` and the client gets an error response, even though the profile is already saved. A client that sees an error will often retry, and the retry creates a second profile. The senior review (finding 3) flags exactly this: a non-critical side effect is coupled to the client's outcome.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a 201 because recording runs after the response is sent**: the response is built but not returned yet; `return response` comes after the awaited call.
- **the write is rolled back**: nothing undoes the create. There is no transaction around these calls.
- **a 201 with a warning header**: no code adds such a header. The failure goes to the `catch` path.

excerpts.quote: await recordVersionUsage({ request, version: apiContext.version, session: apiContext.session, responseStatus: response.status }); return response;
A metrics failure after a successful create or update returns an error to the client, and a retry may then duplicate the write.

notes.title: Why an explicit false survives the v2 adapter
notes.body:
The v2 branch of `toCanonicalUpdateInput` creates an empty `canonical` object and assigns each field only when the payload value is `!== undefined`. `false` is not `undefined`, so `marketingOptIn: false` is copied. Every other field was omitted, so nothing else is added. The patch is `{ marketingOptIn: false }` and nothing more. This is the guide's headline example of presence: false means "turn it off", omitted means "leave it".

Why the others are wrong:
- **{} because false counts as not provided**: that would be the bug of using a truthiness check like `if (payload.marketingOptIn)`. The code compares with `undefined` instead.
- **adds lifecycleState ACTIVE**: lifecycle is only copied when the caller sent it.
- **{ marketingOptIn: undefined }**: the value is copied as-is, and the caller sent `false`.

excerpts.quote: if (modernPayload.marketingOptIn !== undefined) canonical.marketingOptIn = modernPayload.marketingOptIn;
A v2 `{marketingOptIn: false}` becomes `{marketingOptIn: false}`; a v1 email-only update has no name keys.

notes.title: Guards, then the write, then the audit
notes.body:
Read `updateProfile` top to bottom. It loads the existing profile, then runs three guards: `assertCanMutateProfile`, `assertValidUpdateInput` and `assertValidLifecycleTransition`. Only after all three pass does it call `repository.update`. The audit record comes last. This is "validate before each side effect": if any guard throws, no row changes and no audit entry is written, so a rejected request leaves no trace.

Why the others are wrong:
- **update first, guards on the stored result**: checking after writing means the bad data is already saved.
- **audit first**: the review says audit metadata belongs after a successful repository operation. Logging first would record changes that may never happen.
- **lifecycle checks after the write**: `assertValidLifecycleTransition` runs before `repository.update`, as one of the three guards.

excerpts.quote: assertCanMutateProfile(session, existing); assertValidUpdateInput(input); assertValidLifecycleTransition(existing, input.lifecycleState); const updated = await this.repository.update(profileId, input);
audit metadata belongs after a successful repository operation.

notes.title: Why a one-word name gets the family name Unknown
notes.body:
On create, v1's `fullName` goes through `splitFullName`. It trims, splits on whitespace, takes the first part as `givenName` and joins the rest as `familyName`. For "Cher" the rest is empty, `rest.join(" ")` is the empty string, and `|| "Unknown"` replaces it. So v2 later reads givenName 'Cher', familyName 'Unknown'. The guide calls v1 compatibility intentionally lossy: v1 cannot say "no family name", so the adapter fills one in.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a 400 error**: nothing requires two name parts; a single word is accepted.
- **givenName '' and familyName 'Cher'**: the first word becomes the given name, not the family name.
- **familyName '' (empty)**: the empty string is falsy, so `||` swaps it for "Unknown".

excerpts.quote: const [givenName, ...rest] = fullName.trim().split(/\s+/);
familyName: rest.join(" ") || "Unknown"

notes.title: Why padded undefined keys make the audit lie
notes.body:
The audit record in `updateProfile` stores `changedFields: Object.keys(input)`. `Object.keys` lists every key that exists on the object, including keys whose value is `undefined`. If an adapter padded the patch with every optional field set to `undefined`, Prisma might skip those values on write, but the audit row would still claim that every field changed. The guide's point is that the audit trail must describe the effective change, so the patch must only contain keys the caller really sent.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Prisma writes NULL**: the question itself grants that Prisma skips undefined values; the problem is elsewhere.
- **JSON.stringify throws**: `JSON.stringify` does not throw on undefined values; it leaves those keys out.
- **Zod rejects the patch**: the guide's objection is about audit and fake persistence behaviour, not schema validation.

excerpts.quote: changedFields: Object.keys(input)
Padding every optional key with `undefined` makes audit and fake persistence behavior misleading even if Prisma later skips undefined values.

notes.title: Why the rollout gate can be gamed
notes.body:
`stableBucket` adds up the character codes of `clientId` and takes the remainder mod 100. A caller is let in when that bucket is below the rollout percentage. But `clientId` comes from the `x-client-id` request header, which the caller writes. Anyone can try different ids until the sum lands under the percentage. Summing characters also spreads clients poorly (ids with the same letters in any order land in the same bucket). The senior review records this as finding 4.

Why the others are wrong:
- **allowlist uses startsWith**: the allowlist check is `includes` on an array, which is an exact match.
- **percentages above 100 disable the check**: a bucket is always 0-99, so a percentage over 100 would let everyone in rather than disable anything, and the review does not name this.
- **Math.random**: the bucket is deterministic; there is no randomness to retry against.

excerpts.quote: return [...clientId].reduce((sum, character) => sum + character.charCodeAt(0), 0) % 100;
const clientId = request.headers.get("x-client-id");
`clientId` is caller-chosen, so the rollout gate is trivially bypassable and poorly distributed.

notes.title: Why every authorization rule here is advisory
notes.body:
The services check role and ownership carefully, but those checks trust the session object. `requireSession` builds that object straight from request headers: `x-user-id`, `x-user-role` and `x-client-id`. Nothing is signed. Any caller can send `x-user-role: ADMIN` and every role check then passes. So the rules are only as strong as the headers, which is why the review calls them advisory until a signed session or token replaces this adapter. The code's own comment says it is for learning only.

Why the others are wrong:
- **roles cached per process**: there is no cache; the role is read from the headers on each request.
- **checks skipped in development**: no `NODE_ENV` switch appears in this flow.
- **checks run after the write**: `updateProfile` runs its guards before `repository.update`.

excerpts.quote: const role = request.headers.get("x-user-role") as UserRole | null;
This header-based adapter is for learning only; production code should derive identity from a signed session or token.
Any caller can claim `ADMIN`, which makes every authorization rule in the services advisory until a signed session replaces this adapter.

notes.title: Why clients without a version header land on v1
notes.body:
The version registry marks v1 with `isDefault: true`, and the same entry says `lifecycle: "DEPRECATED"`. A request with no `x-api-version` header gets the default, so it gets v1, the old contract that is scheduled to go away. Clients that never send the header keep landing on v1 and never notice they need to migrate until the default is switched. The senior review lists this as finding 7.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a 400 because the header is mandatory**: the registry defines a default precisely so a missing header is allowed.
- **v2 as the newest version**: "newest" is not the rule; the `isDefault` flag decides, and it is on v1.
- **the rollout bucket decides**: rollout controls whether a client may use a version, not which version a missing header picks.

excerpts.quote: lifecycle: "DEPRECATED", isDefault: true,
The default version is the deprecated one, so clients that send no version keep landing on v1 until the default is switched.
